records.name: Artjoms
records.facts_used: The Latvian dictionary lists Artjoms as a form of Artemijs. Its proposed origin account compares the family with Greek artemēs, unharmed or safe. On 16 September 2010 Artjoms Rudņevs scored all three Lech Poznań goals against Juventus in Turin in the Europa League. His last strike came in added time to secure a 3–3 draw. UEFA reported the match as his hat-trick evening.

records.name: Deniss

Changes across languages explain how the ancient Greek family is also recognised in the shorter spelling Deniss. Figure skater Deniss Vasiļjevs won European Championship bronze in 2022. The International Skating Union identifies him as Latvia’s first skater to medal at that championship. He also won silver at the John Wilson Trophy Grand Prix that year.

The National Museum of Art catalogue preserves the sitter’s account of working as a milkmaid at Reči farm beside her portrait. The museum holds a silver gelatin print.

records.name: Irēna
records.facts_used: Irēna is based on Greek eirēnē, peace. In Greek mythology Eirene personifies peace. This connection explains the name’s traditional meaning and its place in the international Irene family, which developed different spellings across languages. Translator and lexicographer Irēna Birzvalka’s first translated work was Zofia Posmysz’s novella Pasažiere, published by Liesma in 1966. She translated from Polish, English and Russian and also helped compile bilingual dictionaries.
records.reason: A checked dictionary or rendering reference and a concrete dated calendar, cultural, literary, sporting or institutional episode support two paragraphs in all five product languages.
records.uncertainties: Greek peace is distinguished from the translator’s professional history. The 1966 book is identified as her first published translation according to the institutional biography.

records.name: Jekaterina
records.facts_used: Jekaterina without a macron is documented beside Єкатерина in the Ukrainian-name rendering manual. This establishes a specific rendering. The Greek origin of the international Katherine family is disputed; the pure interpretation reflects a later association with katharos. The family has a specific name-change story: German princess Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst adopted Екатерина in 1744 before marrying the future Russian emperor Peter III. She later ruled as Catherine II, known as Catherine the Great.

records.uncertainties: The Ukrainian rendering manual explicitly pairs Єкатерина with Jekaterina on page 156. It does not establish every Latvian borrowing route. Katherine has an uncertain Greek origin; purity is a later association. Catherine II adopted Екатерина, not the Latvian spelling.

records.name: Liene
records.facts_used: The dictionary treats Liene and Liena together under Helēna. This family’s Greek root is not securely settled; comparisons include helene, torch, as a folk etymology. A single light-related meaning therefore cannot be presented as a proven origin. The Latvian Language Agency’s 2019 Valodas prakse collection cites Liene as an example of literary and cinematic influence. Known in Vidzeme since 1740, it became especially popular after the film adaptation of the Kaudzīte brothers’ Mērnieku laiki.

records.uncertainties: The Liene/Liena dictionary entry refers to Helēna, whose Greek root remains uncertain. The 2019 language-practice volume, page 153, gives Liene in Vidzeme in 1740 and later film-related popularity. No unverified film release or cast detail is added.

An English translation appeared in Wales in 2018; that same year Latvia saw her second collection, Dzērājmeitiņa. These are specific milestones in a bearer’s literary career.

records.name: Maija
records.facts_used: The dictionary entry for Maija preserves several possibilities: a link with Marija, Greek and Roman Maia, or Vedic Māyā. These are distinct proposals. It gives a Latvian attestation in 1506 and a calendar entry in 1782. Anna Brigadere published the fairy-tale play Maija un Paija with Valters un Rapa in 1921. It premiered at the National Theatre on 15 November 1922, directed by Aleksis Mierlauks. Maija thus also became the name of a Latvian stage character.

records.uncertainties: Marija, Greek/Roman Maia and Vedic Māyā are distinct proposed connections, not a single proven derivation. Publication in 1921 and premiere in 1922 are different events.

His art centre in Daugavpils Fortress opened on 24 April 2013. Cooperation with the artist’s children made it possible to exhibit original works from the family collection in the city.

The name thus also appears in the history of Latvian theatre scholarship.

records.name: Paula
records.facts_used: Paula is the feminine form of Pauls; Latin paulus means small. The Latvian dictionary catalogue suggests an early attestation at Bērzmuiža in 1878 and gives a calendar entry in 1915. The possible nature of the early record is retained. Painter Paula Modersohn-Becker bore the same international form. Her commemorative building on Bremen’s Böttcherstraße opened on 2 June 1927. Originally named Paula-Becker-Modersohn-Haus, it was designed by her artist friend Bernhard Hoetger.

Film and theatre scholar Valentīna Freimane published Ardievu, Atlantīda! in 2010, recalling childhood in Riga, Paris and Berlin and survival during the Holocaust. Its continuation, Antigones likums, appeared posthumously in 2024.
